name: Pramiracetam

lead: Pramiracetam is a racetam, a relative of piracetam, taken by mouth to support memory and concentration. It has been sold as a medicine in some European countries for memory and attention problems in older adults.
People interested in looks use it indirectly: better focus can mean steadier study, work and training routines.

paras: How it works is not settled. Research points to cholinergic effects and interactions with adrenal steroids, and animal studies show an inverted-U dose response.
Reviews describe racetams as very low in toxicity, and a volunteer trial saw no significant side effects. Mild headache, nausea or insomnia are reported. It is not FDA-approved.

chain: Claimed support for focus, memory and mental energy
More consistent studying, training and routines
angle.text: Users take pramiracetam as a cognition aid, hoping for better concentration and recall during demanding days. Any link to appearance runs through that indirect chain of focus and consistency rather than a direct effect on the body.

lead: Pramiracetam is a synthetic nootropic of the racetam family, derived from piracetam and taken by mouth. People who use it for self-improvement are mainly after sharper focus, memory and mental stamina, which feed into study, work and training consistency and, through those, the habits that go into a better physique and appearance [1][2].

It was developed by Parke-Davis in the late 1970s and has been marketed as a prescription medicine in a few European countries, for example as Pramistar, for memory and attention problems in older adults. It has not been approved by the US FDA for any indication [3].

Published research includes a small randomized placebo-controlled trial in young men with memory problems after head injury or oxygen deprivation, pharmacokinetic work in healthy volunteers, a small Alzheimer's study, and a body of animal studies [4][5][6][7].
infobox: Not FDA-approved; prescription medicine in some European countries [3]

paras: In medicine, pramiracetam has been used and studied for memory and attention problems in older adults and for cognitive deficits after traumatic brain injury [1][4]. In Italy it was sold by Menarini as Pramistar until the marketing authorization was withdrawn at the manufacturer's request in 2020; it remains listed in Latvia [3].
Healthy adults also take it as a nootropic for memory and focus. Controlled studies in unimpaired people are scarce [3].

A pharmacokinetic trial gave single oral doses to healthy male volunteers in a double-blind randomized design; peak levels came 2 to 3 hours after dosing, half-life was 4.5 to 6.5 hours, and no significant side effects were observed at any dose [5].

A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in young males with memory problems after head injury or anoxia reported clinically significant improvement in memory measures, especially delayed recall, compared with placebo [4].

A small two-phase trial in 10 patients with probable Alzheimer's disease found that eight showed a best dose in the first phase, but only two improved to a similar degree on replication [6]. A trial in healthy volunteers examined effects on scopolamine-induced amnesia [8]. Reviews describe pramiracetam as reportedly improving cognitive deficits linked to traumatic brain injury [1].

The mechanism is not settled. Reviews of piracetam-type nootropics describe an interaction with cholinergic systems, and note that parallel experiments with different racetams sometimes give divergent results [9][10]. Pramiracetam increased high-affinity choline uptake in rat hippocampal tissue [11], inhibited the enzyme prolyl endopeptidase in vitro [12], and, as with other racetams, its memory effects in animals depended on adrenal steroids [10][13]. Animal dose-response curves are inverted-U shaped [6].
In volunteers, peak concentrations and exposure rose linearly with dose, and clearance and half-life were independent of dose [5].

Reviews describe racetams as having very low toxicity and lacking serious side effects [2]. No significant side effects were seen in the volunteer pharmacokinetic trial up to 1,600 mg single doses [5]. Headache, nausea, dizziness, insomnia and stomach upset have been reported as mild effects [3].
